title: High versus standard power direct selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) in open angle glaucoma
official: High vs. standard power in direct selective laser trabeculoplasty (DSLT) in patients with ocular hypertension (OHT) and glaucoma – a single centre randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
The aim of this study is to compare two different strengths of Direct Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (DSLT), a laser treatment used to lower eye pressure in people with ocular hypertension or glaucoma. The study will assess whether a higher-power treatment is more effective than the standard-power treatment at reducing eye pressure.

People who choose to take part will be asked to sign a consent form before any study procedures begin. A baseline assessment will then be carried out, including measuring eye pressure before treatment.

For participants receiving treatment in both eyes, one eye will receive the standard-power DSLT treatment and the other eye will receive the higher-power DSLT treatment. Neither the participant nor the study staff carrying out follow-up assessments will know which treatment each eye received. This helps ensure that the study results are fair and unbiased.
Participants will be followed for 12 months after treatment. During this time, their eye pressure and eye health will be monitored. If the laser treatment does not adequately control eye pressure, additional treatment may be offered, including further laser treatment or prescription eye drops, in line with standard clinical care. 

Who can participate? 
Patients aged 18 years and over with ocular hypertension and/or glaucoma who are currently not on eye pressure lowering treatment or those who are using a single eye drop to lower their eye pressure. 

What does the study involve? 
If someone chooses to take part in this study, they will first attend a baseline clinic visit to check whether the treatment is suitable for them. During this visit, the study team will ask about their medical history and carry out a number of routine eye tests. These include measuring vision and eye pressure, examining the front of the eye, checking the eye's drainage angle (gonioscopy), testing peripheral vision, and taking OCT scans, which are detailed images of the back of the eye. In some cases, existing eye medications may need to be stopped for a short period before treatment.

On the day of treatment, eye pressure will be checked before the procedure and eye drops will be given to help prevent a rise in pressure. After treatment, eye pressure will be checked again about one hour later. If everything is satisfactory, the participant can go home. Additional eye drops may be prescribed if needed.

Participants will be followed up for 12 months after treatment. Visits are planned approximately 1 week, 2 months, 6 months, and 12 months after treatment to monitor eye health and assess the effect of the treatment. Some participants may be asked to attend additional visits if closer monitoring is required. Participants will also be asked whether they would like to be contacted about future research studies. Agreeing to be contacted does not mean they have to take part in any future research, and they can choose not to be contacted at any time. The baseline assessment and treatment visit are expected to take around 3 hours, while follow-up visits are expected to take around 2 hours each.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
The laser treatment used in this study is designed to lower eye pressure in people with glaucoma or ocular hypertension. Lowering eye pressure may help protect vision and reduce the need for eye drops. However, the treatment may not work for everyone, and its effects may wear off over time.

Most people do not experience serious problems after treatment. Possible side effects include:
•	Mild discomfort or irritation in the eye for a few days after treatment.
•	A temporary increase in eye pressure, which may require treatment with eye drops.
•	Temporary blurred vision caused by inflammation inside the eye (this is rare).
•	A small red patch on the white of the eye, which is usually painless and clears on its own.
•	Redness, watering, sensitivity to light, or a feeling of irritation in the eye.
•	A mild headache for a short time after treatment.
•	If the laser treatment does not lower eye pressure enough, or if its effect wears off, additional treatment may be offered. 

This could include repeat laser treatment or prescription eye drops as part of normal care.

Where is the study run from? 
The study is run at Moorfields Eye Hospital, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
November and will run for 2 years and 6 months (30 months) to October 2028.

Who is funding the study? 
Alcon Eye Care Limited

Who is the main contact? 
1. Jade Barnfield, Clinical Trials Research Manager, NIHR Clinical Research Facility, jade.barnfield1@nhs.net
2. Research and innovation at Moorfields Eye Hospital, moorfields.resadmin@nhs.net

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Age over 18 years and able to provide informed consent
2.	Diagnosis of OHT requiring bilateral treatment as per nice guidelines or POAG requiring bilateral treatment
3.	No previous treatment or on one single eye drop for OHT or POAG
4.	A medicated IOP of < =  31 mmHg at the screening visit
5.	An unmedicated IOP of < =  34 mmHg at the screening visit
6.	For eyes with OHT the washed out IOP value must be > =  24 mmHg and < =  34 mmHg 
7.	For eyes with OAG the washed out diurnal IOP value must be > =  22 mmHg and < =  34 mmHg 
8.	Able to provide informed written consent to participate in the study
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Advanced glaucoma either eye as determined by EMGT criteria: visual field loss mean deviation worse than -12dB in the better or -15dB in the worse eye
2.	Secondary glaucoma (e.g. pigment dispersion syndrome, pseudoexfoliation, rubeosis, trauma etc) or any angle closure. 
3.	Previous medical treatment for POAG/OHT with more than one pharmaccological agent
4.	Previous laser or surgical treatment for OAG or OHT 
5.	Any contraindication to SLT (e.g. unable to tolerate speculum, past history of or active uveitis), inability to use topical medical therapy because of, for example, physical infirmity and a lack of carers able to administer daily eyedrops
6.	Any history of retinal ischaemia, macular oedema or diabetic retinopathy
7.	Active retinal pathology, e.g. AMD, DR etc
8.	Visual acuity worse than 6/36 in a study eye. Non-progressive visual loss better than 6/36 due to any comorbidity is permitted provided that it does not affect response to treatment or later surgical choices and is not under active follow-up (e.g. an old, isolated retinal scar no longer under review, amblyopia).
9.	Any previous intra-ocular surgery, except uncomplicated phaco-emulsification at least one year before
10.	Any previous intra-ocular surgery, except uncomplicated phaco-emulsification at least 6 months before
11.	Medically unfit for completion of the trial – e.g. suffering from a terminal illness or too unwell to be able to attend hospital clinic visits
12.	Recent involvement in another interventional research study (within 3 months)
